title: Check yourself: what the compiler allows an exception class to be

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: Per this page, what happens to `class GenericException<T> extends Exception`?

options.text: It compiles, and a catch clause matches the erased type
options.says: The page says the declaration itself is rejected, because a catch clause could never check the type argument at run time.

options.text: It compiles, and each type argument is caught separately
options.says: Type erasure makes every parameterization one run-time class, which is why the page says the compiler rejects the declaration.

options.text: It is rejected, since erasure would defeat the catch clause
options.says: The page quotes the compiler's message, "a generic class may not extend java.lang.Throwable", and gives erasure as the reason.

questions.stem: Per this page, why declare `private static final long serialVersionUID` in an exception class?

options.text: So recompiling the class does not change its computed serial version
options.says: Every exception is Serializable through Throwable; a declared serialVersionUID keeps the version stable when instances cross a remote call or a cache.

options.text: So the exception class becomes Serializable and can cross a remote call
options.says: The page says every exception is already Serializable, because Throwable implements the interface.

options.text: So fields of types that are not Serializable can still be written out
options.says: The page says to keep extra fields serializable; the field does not rescue a field that is not.

concepts: An exception class cannot be generic, and a record cannot be an exception.
Every exception is Serializable, so one that may be serialized declares a serialVersionUID.
